newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines meets with pilots as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines meets with pilots as strike looms.

text.p: Senior executives at American Airlines met with pilots' union leaders on Thursday but, as expected, there was no breakthrough in their efforts to stave off a damaging strike that could start as early as next week.
The two sides met for four hours at the carrier's headquarters in Fort Worth, Texas, to explain the positions they will take into full-scale negotiations due to begin in Washington on Monday.
"As we expected, it was a useful opportunity to exchange information and get some homework done ahead of next week," said Allied Pilots Association spokesman Gregg Overman.

American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp. , described the meeting as a "cordial exchange of information" and said in a statement that management had again urged the pilots to accept binding arbitration in the bitter labour dispute.

Pilots' leaders say they want to win a new contract now, even if it involves strike action, rather than risk lengthy arbitration and insist they will shut down the airline from Feb. 15 unless a deal is reached before then.
A senior union leader, asking not to be identified, said he sees a 50 percent possibility of strike action, and that it could last up to 60 days.

Starting Monday, the two sides are to begin five days of "supermediation" in a last-gasp effort to reach a new four-year labour contract. Those negotiations will take place in Washington with the help of the National Mediation Board.

Pilots are demanding pay raises of more than 11 percent over the life of the contract, improved stock options and a guarantee that American will not use its American Eagle commuter carrier, which employs pilots of another union, to fly 50-passenger regional jets.

In a tentative agreement reached last September, the airline offered a 5 percent wage increase over four years and stock options. But it reserved the right to equip American Eagle with regional jets. Pilots' union leaders at first accepted that deal, but rank-and-file members rejected it in a surprise vote last month.
American Airlines said the pilots' new demands would cost the carrier an additional $200 million per year and would destroy its efforts to remain competitive.
The APA disputes that figure, saying its proposal would cost an additional $285 million over five years.
Both sides explained their conflicting cost analyses at Thursday's meeting, which was attended by airline President Don Carty, Chief Financial Officer Gerard Arpey and APA President Jim Sovich.
"The idea is that both sides know where we stand so we don't stumble into a strike because of any misunderstanding," the union official said.

The threat of strike action has already pushed many American Airlines customers to make alternative bookings for travel in February and March, and the carrier could suffer huge losses if shut down by a walkout.
Despite the strike threat, AMR's stock gained $1.625 to $80.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
